Interim Discussion Study 2

Mirroring study 1, Machiavellianism and psychopathy showed weak positive correlations with MCT malevolence. As the strongest, yet non-significant correlation with MCT creativity metrics, sadism showed a positive link to MCT originality (r = 0.11). Additionally, narcissism weakly positively correlated with MCT fluency, but this link vanished in multiple regression models. Yet, in these models, a significant three-way interaction of sadism x psychopathy x Machiavellianism emerged, showing that malevolent creativity was higher in individuals who reported a combination of higher sadism, higher Machiavellianism, and higher psychopathy. Critically, this effect was small with f² = 0.02. Other dark tetrad interaction effects emerged for MCT malevolence, originality, and fluency, mainly including links of higher sadism with higher MCT scores, combined with lower expressions of Machiavellianism and psychopathy. However overall, these patterns for MCT subscales were rather inconsistent, and no effect exceeded f² = 0.02.

GENERAL DISCUSSION

The goal of the present study was to review and extend evidence on previously reported associations of the dark triad/tetrad and malevolent creativity, following the idea that the relevance of the dark tetrad for malevolent creativity may have been overstated. In two independent studies, we tested whether individuals higher in narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, or sadism exhibited a higher capacity for generating malevolent creative ideas in a performance test, as has often been inferred from large correlations of these dark traits with self-reported malevolent creativity (see Gao et al., 2022; Geng et al., 2024; Jia et al., 2020; Silva et al., 2025; Szabó et al., 2022). Although study 1 examined the dark triad, and study 2 the dark tetrad, for brevity reasons, we will subsequently discuss our findings referring to the dark tetrad.

In both our studies, neither aspect of the dark tetrad displayed correlations larger than r = .10 with our composite metric of total malevolent creativity, and no correlation reached significance. As the number of harmful revenge ideas also rated as original, total malevolent creativity reflects malevolent divergent thinking, i.e., coming up with a large pool of harmful original ideas, which research argues, maximizes chances of creatively hurting others in versatile ways (Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2021ab, 2022ab). Accordingly, we find no evidence that higher scores on either aspect of the dark tetrad alone relate to a higher potential for overall malevolent creativity when prompted to come up with creative revenge ideas for unfair social situations. Here, one may question the focus on generating many original ideas for harm, as in real-life, people may become deeply invested in elaborating and refining one highly harmful and original idea. However, dark tetrad correlations with other-rated originality of ideas were equally non-significant. Here, the largest correlation emerged for sadism and originality of ideas (r = .11), with this effect turning partially significant in multiple regression models. Overall, our nonsignificant and negligible associations of narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism with creativity in harmful idea generation challenge the status quo of malevolent creativity research. In the following, we discuss this from three different perspectives that may be useful for future investigations on the matter.

Explanation 1: There simply is no direct link of single dark tetrad aspects with malevolent creativity Given our findings, we need to consider that individuals scoring higher on single aspects of the dark tetrad do in fact not have a meaningfully higher capacity for malevolent creativity, although given their malevolent nature, we may have been led to believe that they do. Previously, it has been argued that higher sadism may be especially relevant for malevolent creativity, as sadism is defined by enjoyment of suffering of others, despite lack of a personal relationship or contempt for the victim (e.g., Dow, 2023; Buckels et al., 2013). As underlined by high correlations with bullying, malicious pranks, or online harassment of strangers (Ward, 2025), individuals higher in sadism delight in causing anybody harm.

This, as proposed by Dow (2023), they may achieve this through surprising and original means that catch others off guard, e.g., in the online world, by cyberstalking, doxing, catfishing, trolling, and generally terrorizing others for personal pleasure. However, as we will discuss below, the degree of sadism relevant for such behaviors may be rather different that was is measured within a normal range of dark tetrad questionnaires applied in normal populations. In support, in our malevolent creativity test, links of sadism and originality of ideas on our malevolent creativity test were trivial (r = 0.11), and more closely aligned with previous null findings for originality in deception tasks (Kapoor et al., 2025 (Kapoor et al., , 2026) ) than with presumably inflated correlations with malevolent creativity self-report (up to r = 0.72, Wang et al., 2026). In sum, although we obtained partially significant associations of sadism with originality of ideas in multiple regression models, given the size of the effect (f² = 0.02), it is in doubt whether elevated sadism in nonclinical samples is truly meaningful in describing, and predicting, individuals' potential for creative harm.

Still, our regression models also allowed to test whether interactions of dark tetrad, i.e., higher expressions on multiple traits may be more relevant for malevolent creativity than higher scores on single traits. In study 1, no significant interactions of the dark triad on malevolent creativity emerged, indicating that not even a combination of higher narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy explained variance in malevolent creativity. However, in study 2, sadism changed this pattern, as threeway interactions of Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism predicted total malevolent creativity, as well as originality and malevolence of ideas. The three-way interaction of higher expressions on all traits on total malevolent creativity presented the strongest effect that was however, still small in effect size terms (β = 0.27, f² = 0.02). Interpreted together with correlational results for sadism, this suggests that higher instrumental thinking and strategic manipulation of others (Machiavellianism) as well as higher callousness, impulsivity, and lack of remorse (psychopathy) may not matter much for malevolent creativity by themselves. Machiavellianism may not directly correlate with malevolent creativity, presumably because (negative) relationships are managed in very careful, strategic ways, depending on risks and gains of a situation (see Paulhus, 2014). Similarly, individuals higher in psychopathy may show a stronger propensity for direct, and thus, effective aggression (Paulhus et al., 2018), with no perceived added value of creativity. In fact, we may argue that if individuals only present elevated levels of (subclinical) psychopathy, they may care less for deception, trickery, and covering their tracks, and for this reason, show lower creativity. This is also underlined by negative links of psychopathy to originality in our multiple regression models. Yet, if higher sadism, and thus, the appetitive motivation to harm others for enjoyment, is added to the mix, strategic manipulation of Machiavellianism and callous impulsivity of psychopathy may contribute small, but meaningful ingredients for total malevolent creativity. In general, our results are compatible with research findings that individuals with combinations of elevated dark triad/tetrad traits show more risky, deviant, and antisocial behaviors (Chabrol et al., 2015; Maheux-Caron et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2020). As such, when it comes to dark personality, malevolent creativity may be best understood as emerging from an intricate constellation of antagonistic, impulsive, and manipulative traits. This may explain why previous studies have obtained significant associations of composite antisocial personality measures with individuals' capacity for malevolent creativity in tests. For example, Perchtold-Stefan et al. (2021a) reported that the DSM-5 maladaptive personality domain antagonism, encompassing grandiosity, manipulativeness, and deceitfulness, uniquely and positively predicted total malevolent creativity (also see Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2023). Similarly, a combination of higher trait aggression and higher impulsivity has also been linked to higher malevolent creativity performance in other studies (Harris & Reiter-Palmon, 2015). Still, in case of our "triple negative" dark tetrad interaction of Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism on malevolent creativity, the practical relevance of this effect must be questioned, which leads us to explanation 2.

Explanation 2: Investigated samples are simply too "normal", and not malevolent/creative enough

As another perspective on our modest findings, research may have also rather persistently looked at the "wrong" people when scrutinizing dark tetrad links to malevolent creativity (Cropley, 2025). As such, the vast majority of malevolent creativity studies have been conducted in student populations that naturally, mostly show subclinical expressions of dark tetrad traits. However, these are often discussed as if they met clinical thresholds for aversive cognitions and behaviors, including devastating malevolent creativity. Yet, when looking at mean and maximum scores of malevolence on administered malevolent creativity tests or items, it seems that most tested individuals only generate ideas of moderate malevolence. For example, in our study 1, only ~ 17 percent of participants presented average malevolence ratings higher than 3 (out of 6), while for study 2, it was only ~ 3 percent. Importantly, this is no exception when looking at metrics of previous studies (see Batey et al., 2022; Kapoor et al., 2025 Kapoor et al., , 2026;; Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2026). Together with often similarly modest scores for originality, we should thus consider that a large portion of tested individuals are simply not malevolent or creative enough, and thus, too "normal" to expect strong links of antisocial personality with malevolent creativity. This is also corroborated by studies showing that the base-rate of an aversive personality constellation like elevated Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism, as reflected in our three-way interaction on malevolent creativity, is likely low. Running latent profile analyses on personality in the workplace, She et al. (2025) found that 16% of their sample scored high on all aspects of the dark triad.

In a study on high-school students by Chabrol et al. (2015), 15% of the sample were grouped into a high dark tetrad cluster. By comparison, in a community sample from Gómez-Leal et al. (2024), only seven percent scored high on all aspects of the dark tetrad. While these percentages only serve as rough estimates regarding the prevalence of elevated dark tetrad traits, for our argument, they underline that individuals high in Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism only represent a minor portion of the general population. Naturally, low prevalence does not imply low relevance. Still, the idea that a small subgroup of individuals account for a substantial amount of creative harm in daily life is also rebuffed by research on emotional and social factors in malevolent creativity. A variety of studies find that malevolent creativity can be elicited by negative emotions, conflict, threat, or negative environments in general, irrespective of antisocial personality traits (see Baas et al. 2019; Fousiani et al., 2025; Gutworth et al., 2018; Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2024b). Additionally, it can be argued that the prevalence of malevolent creativity in daily life (lies, bullying, defamation, theft, pranks, sabotage, assault) is much higher than the range of action of a few severely antisocial personality profiles. In sum, a configuration of high Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism may well be informative for understanding certain individuals' capacity for malevolent creativity, particularly when it comes to more extreme instances of harm, terrorism, warfare, or crime (see Hunter et al., 2022). However, our findings (and their effect sizes) suggest that the relevance of subclinical dark tetrad expressions specifically may have been overemphasized by malevolent creativity research conducted in student and general population samples.

As one outline for future studies, it may be time to investigate dark personality -malevolent creativity links in populations more relevant to the matter: individuals who are either highly creative, or individuals who are capable of truly harmful actions towards others, or ideally, both.

Explanation 3: Previous research may have not measured malevolent creativity

Finally, we argue that previous research's overemphasis of the dark tetrad for malevolent creativity is likely due to misinterpretations of associations found for malevolent creativity self-report, and partially, misinterpretations of single indices in malevolent creativity tests, like malevolence of ideas.

Regarding the former, findings with the frequently used MCBS are now increasingly challenged, due to the questionnaires' negligible correlations with indicators of creativity (e.g., openness, creative selfefficacy, see Cropley, 2026). A recent examination by Cropley (2026) suggests that the MCBS is predominantly a measure of malevolent ideation, but does not qualify as a measure of creativity.

Accordingly, moderate to large correlations among the dark tetrad the MCBS "malevolent creativity", some even bordering on redundancy (Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026), are unsurprising, as the dark tetrad naturally displays more antisocial, deceptive, or aggressive behaviors (Azizli et al., 2016; Moor & Anderson, 2019; Paulhus et al., 2018). However crucially, as noted by Hunter et al. (2022), neither deception, nor deviance, or crime and law breaking are malevolent creativity, if they are not creative (for similar arguments on aggression, see Harris & Reiter-Palmon, 2015). In this respect, links of the dark tetrad and the MCBS may likely just be malevolence measures correlating with each other, and it should be considered that both have little to do with creativity. Corroborating this idea, when more substantial correlations of the dark tetrad with malevolent creativity on performance tests emerged, they only did so for other-rated malevolence, i.e., antisocial individuals generating ideas that are more harmful (see Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2024a; Kapoor et al., 2025 Kapoor et al., , 2026)). This is also reflected in our studies, where the largest effect was observed for links of sadism and malevolence of ideas in study 2 (r = 0.20). Accordingly, it may be the case that individuals higher in the dark tetrad self-report more malevolent ideation, and also generate more harmful ideas on malevolent creativity tasks, but still lack the originality required for malevolent creativity. Overall, in light of these arguments and our own findings, if the subclinical dark tetrad signals malevolent creativity, it appears to be so little that it may be irrelevant. This calls for the development of better self-report scales for malevolent creativity behavior, and in general, more refined batteries for malevolent idea generation.

Limitations and Outlook

In both our studies, our samples were similar in age, gender composition (more women than men), and were highly educated. Both studies also featured the same malevolent creativity task, with identical instructions, timings, and rating of ideas. Still, as a limitation, in study 1, the MCT was administered in person, while in study 2, it was administered via an online survey, which may complicate comparisons.

As another limitations, our findings are based on specific, short scales of the dark triad and tetrad. As such, our ideas and results should be further scrutinized with more extensive measures. Still, previous research on malevolent creativity and dark personality also seems to have largely relied on short scales (see Table 1). It is also possible that single aspects of the dark tetrad are more meaningfully linked to malevolent creativity if test scenarios more closely reflect particularities of the respective trait. For example, narcissism may result in higher originality of ideas if test situations threaten ego, status, or resources (see Jones & Paulhus, 2010), while sadism may be more strongly related to unprovoked malevolent creativity, i.e., aggressing against unsuspecting weaker targets, even at a personal cost (Buckels et al., 2013). Finally, our discussions only pertain to individuals' capacity for malevolent idea generation (potential) and cannot infer if certain dark tetrad traits would also lead to higher malevolent innovation. While it also seems intuitive that individuals scoring higher in these traits would also more likely implement malevolent creative ideas in real-life (see Wang et al., 2025, for findings with the Malevolent Innovative Behavior Scale), future malevolent creativity tests should be expanded with idea rating protocols to determine the role of the dark tetrad in idea selection, and intended implementation (see Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2025).

Conclusion

In two independent studies, we find little evidence that the dark tetrad is meaningfully linked to a higher capacity for malevolent creativity. While study 1 yielded null findings, in study 2, a (presumably very rare) combination of higher Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism predicted total malevolent creativity in multiple regression models. Crucially however, no observed creativity effects exceeded f² = 0.02. These associations appear trivial, especially in light of the huge emphasis placed on the dark tetrad by past malevolent creativity research, and the obtained, often large correlations of dark tetrad traits and malevolent creativity self-report. From our perspective, it thus seems scholars may have overemphasized the relevance of the dark tetrad for malevolent idea generation in the general population, possibly at the expense of other, more relevant personality traits. Importantly, our argument is not that antisocial personality is irrelevant for understanding everyday manifestations of malevolent creativity, but that the dark tetrad specifically may be less important than previously assumed. When it comes to explaining the tremendous variety and perilousness of malevolent creativity in daily-life, perhaps it is time to move on to other darker shores.

MCBS = Malevolent Creativity Behavior Scale; MCT = Malevolent Creativity Task, referring to different versions of asking participants to generate harmful creative ideas to damage others; MSCBTS = Malevolent Sadistic Creativity Behavior Tendencies Scale; DT = Dark Triad; Mach = Machiavellianism, Narc = narcissism, Psy = psychopathy, Sad = sadism. Reports on the MCBS are restricted to the total score, unless only subscale information is available (seeGao et al., 2025; Szabó et al., 2022), then (H) = MCBS hurting, (L) = MCBS lying, (T) = MCBS tricks. For tasks assessing several indices of malevolent creativity (e.g.,Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2024;Kapoor et al., 2025 Kapoor et al., , 2026)), only originality indices are reported.

Table 1.

Summary of studies linking dark triad/tetrad traits with malevolent creativity

This paper is not intended as a systematic or exhaustive review of literature linking the dark triad/tetrad and malevolent creativity measures. While our goal was to represent relevant studies on the matter, we did not include non-peer reviewed work (e.g., theses, conference papers), or papers that included the dark triad/tetrad as moderators or mediators, but did not report simple correlations with malevolent creativity.

This study was part of a larger investigation on consumption of true crime media, which also included measures of personality and malevolent creativity. The malevolent creativity data has previously been published in another article regarding its links to true crime consumption(Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2026), while the dark triad personality data has also been published regarding links to true crime consumption(Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2025). Importantly, this is the first investigation linking malevolent creativity and the dark triad.

This study was part of a larger investigation on perception of ordinary vs. creative aggression, a manuscript which is currently under review. In this project, personality traits like the dark tetrad were assessed to see if they moderated differences in ratings of ordinary vs. creative aggressive behaviors. The current data linking malevolent creativity in a performance test to the dark tetrad has not been published before.
